intro: Nine verses, two of them heading, and one of the shortest complete prayers in the book: three verses of plea, four of confidence, nothing in between. The heading pins it to a real betrayal, the men of Ziph telling Saul where David was hiding, and the psalm never names Saul again. Two things are worth watching. The first is the prefix be-, by or with: God saves by Your name, gives judgment by Your might, and puts an end to enemies by Your truth, three abstract nouns doing the work an army does elsewhere. The second is the ending -ni, me, glued to verb after verb: save me, judge me, delivered me.

stichs.en: For the leader, with stringed music.

verses.summary: A filing label: who performs it, on what instruments, in what genre, by whom. Maskil marks a psalm that means to teach and not only to be sung.

stichs.en: When the Ziphites came and said to Saul:
Is David not hiding himself among us?

verses.summary: The heading quotes the informers in their own words, as a question, which is how someone volunteers information while pretending to ask for it. The psalm that follows never answers them.

stichs.en: God, save me by Your name,
and by Your might give judgment for me.

verses.summary: The whole plea in one breath. Name and might are what David has instead of soldiers, and both verbs carry the same object suffix, me.

stichs.en: give ear to the words of my mouth.

verses.summary: The same request twice, hear and give ear, which is how biblical poetry insists rather than repeats. The second line is more concrete than the first: not prayer in general, the words actually being said.

stichs.en: For strangers have risen against me,
and ruthless men have sought my life;
they have not set God before them. Selah.

verses.summary: The grounds for the plea, and then the diagnosis. The danger is not that the enemies are strong; it is that God is nowhere in their field of view.

stichs.en: the Lord is the sustainer of my life.

verses.summary: The hinge of the psalm. Nothing in the situation has changed and the mood of the verbs changes anyway, from asking to reporting.

stichs.en: He will turn the evil back on those who watch me;
in Your faithfulness, put an end to them.

verses.summary: The one violent line, and it is handed over rather than acted on: the second verb is an imperative addressed to God, not a plan the speaker carries out.

stichs.en: With a freewill offering let me sacrifice to You;
let me thank Your name, LORD, for it is good.

verses.summary: The vow. A freewill offering is the one sacrifice nobody owes, which is exactly why it is the one named here.

stichs.en: For He has delivered me from every trouble,
and my eye has looked on my enemies.

verses.summary: Spoken as already finished while the Ziphites are still talking to Saul. The perfect tense is the entire claim of the psalm.

pardes.body: Two verses of heading, then two halves that mirror each other. Verses 3 to 5 ask and give the reason: strangers have risen, ruthless men want his life, and they do not keep God in view. Verses 6 to 9 answer without any new information having arrived: God is my helper, the harm will turn back, I will bring an offering and thank the name. The heading sends the reader to 1 Samuel 23, where the men of Ziph go up to Saul at Gibeah and tell him David is hiding in their hill country. Ziph is a town of Judah, so the men handing David over are of his own tribe, which makes the word strangers in verse 5 the hardest word on the page.

{{5.1}} means strangers, and that is the Masoretic reading. Some Hebrew manuscripts have instead a word meaning insolent or presumptuous, and the closely parallel opening at Psalm 86:14 has that second word where this verse has the first. Which of the two stood here originally is disputed, and the choice changes the psalm: foreigners attacking, or the arrogant of one's own people. The second crux is {{6.5}}, a plural participle with the preposition attached, literally among the upholders of my life. Hebrew also uses that preposition to say that someone is the thing itself rather than one of a group, which is why most translations read the Lord is the sustainer of my life. Both readings are defended.

Read against 1 Samuel, this is a psalm about betrayal by neighbours rather than attack by outsiders, and the word strangers becomes the reading itself: people of your own tribe who hand you over have made themselves strangers. Notice what the prayer does not do. It never asks for the informers to be punished by name, and the one aggressive line, {{7.0}}, asks only that the harm be turned back along the line it came. The vow of verse 8 is then the measure of the answer. An obligatory sacrifice would prove nothing about the person bringing it; a freewill offering is what gets given when nothing is owed.

The divine names move across the psalm. Verses 3, 4 and 5 say God, verse 6 says God and then the Lord, and only at verse 8, at the vow, does the four letter name appear. Psalm 54 sits inside the long block of psalms that prefer the name God throughout, so a single four letter name at the end carries weight it would not carry elsewhere in the book. Read mystically, the psalm walks from the name associated with strict judgment to the name associated with mercy while the circumstances stay exactly as they were, which means the only thing that moved was the one praying. That is also why the offering promised is freewill: the movement cannot be commanded.
